cerebellar ataxia with inability to stand or walk alone, stiff gait, tension of paravertebral musculature with hyperlordosis, resting tremor of the left arm (greater amplitude that is typical for parkinsonian tremor), discrete resting tremor of the right arm, and diffusely low muscle tonus and muscle strength. Her facial expression was reduced and speech was normal but monotonous. Deep tendon reflexes were present, with normal plantar response. Deficits in sensibility were not found.

The subjective sensation of tremulousness was still present. She seemed anxious and depressed and felt relatively good only while lying on bed, staring at 1 point. Transitory horizontal nystagmus and dilated pupils were occasionally observed and tachycardia (up to 130/min) with tachypnea was present.

Clinical appearance of neurologic dysfunction and the finding of significantly increased levels of anti-GAD autoantibodies provided support for the diagnosis of SPS.

The typical clinical form is characterized by the rigidity of paraspinal muscles with exaggerated lumbar lordosis, muscular spasms caused by internal (eg, emotional distress) or external (eg, noises, movements) stimuli, with otherwise normal findings in motor and sensory examinations and by a continuous motor-unit activity detected by electromyography.

Administration of diazepam in doses up to 40 mg/d did not improve the neurologic status substantially and essential sedation occurred. Persistent disability despite first-line therapy with diazepam indicated the application of corticosteroids (oral methylprednisolone 64 mg/d). According to the clinical global impression the patient seemed to benefit from short-term immunosuppression.
Magnetic resonance imaging of the brain showed somewhat larger third and lateral ventricles with larger frontotemporal bilateral subarachnoid spaces.

The possibility of a paraneoplastic SPS was excluded because screenings and performed examinations showed no evidence of a malignant process. Further more, in paraneoplastic SPS serology tests for anti-GAD antibodies are usually negative. Progressive supranuclear palsy and multiple system atrophy were excluded because of the absence of eye movement abnormalities and orthostatic hypotension. Because of the long duration of the disorder with no evidence of trismus and electrolyte imbalance, there were no signs of tetanus and tetany resulting from electrolyte abnormalities. A lumbar puncture was performed twice in the interval of a week, approximately 40 mL of CSF (the so-called intermittent high volume tap) was taken, this did not relieve the patient’s symptoms, therefore the diagnosis of normal-pressure hydrocephalus was also excluded.
